name: Guarani (Paraguayan)
variety: Paraguayan Guarani (avañeʼẽ) in the standard orthography of Paraguay (achegety)
sources: Estigarribia, Bruno (2020). A Grammar of Paraguayan Guarani. London: UCL Press.
Gregores, Emma & Suárez, Jorge A. (1967). A Description of Colloquial Guaraní. The Hague: Mouton.
Walker, Rachel (1999). Guaraní voiceless stops in oral versus nasal contexts: an acoustical study. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 29(1), 63-94.
Clopper, Cynthia G. & Tonhauser, Judith (2013). The prosody of focus in Paraguayan Guaraní. International Journal of American Linguistics 79(2), 219-251.
Kaiser, Eden (2008). Nasal spreading in Paraguayan Guaraní: introducing long-distance continuous spreading. Amerindia 32.
contrasts: six oral versus six nasal vowels in the stressed syllable: aka 'quarrel' versus akã 'head', pytu 'breath' versus pytũ 'dark', oke 'sleeps' versus okẽ 'door'
words are oral, nasal or nasal-oral as a whole; nasal and prenasalised consonants (m and mb, n and nd, ŋ and ng) alternate with the nasality of the word
stress on the last syllable versus marked earlier stress (tape versus áva)
no voiced oral stops b d g and no trill in native words; l and the retroflex sibilant ʐ (written rr) come from Spanish loans
allophony: nasal harmony: a stressed nasal vowel or a nasal consonant of a root nasalises the sounds to its left in the same word; the effect weakens with distance and is not heard more than about three syllables away
voiceless consonants are transparent to leftward nasalisation: they stay oral and voiceless and do not stop the spread (Walker 1999)
nasalisation also spreads rightwards, usually one syllable only, onto suffixes and enclitics
prenasalised stops nasalise only what precedes them; suffixes with nasals do not nasalise the root; nasalisation does not cross the boundary inside a compound
in nasal words /ʝ/ appears as [ɲ] (written ñ), /ᵐb ⁿd ᵑɡ/ as [m n ŋ], /ɰ/ as nasalised [ɰ̃] (written g̃), and /ʋ ɾ/ are nasalised
/ʝ/ (written j) is a voiced palatal fricative, or a palatal stop or affricate [ɟ ~ dʒ] in careful speech
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant, dropped in some frequent words
/ɰ/ occurs mostly before u, where it is [ɣʷ] or [w]
voiceless stops are unaspirated; p and t have a longer voice onset time in nasal words, k has the longest of the three and is not affected (Walker 1999)
the glottal stop is often dropped in fast speech and frequent words; vowel-initial words begin with a phonetic glottal stop
unstressed high vowels next to another vowel are glides; many vowel sequences are nevertheless two syllables (a.o, ha.i)
syllable_structure: (C)V, with V optionally flanked by glides: V, CV, VV, CVV, CVVV; no codas in native words
phonotactics: prenasalised mb, nd, ng, nt are single onsets; speakers may put the nasal part in the preceding syllable (mem.by)
no consonant clusters in native words; old Spanish loans were adapted (cruz became kurusu), recent ones keep clusters and codas
every diphthong contains an unstressed high vowel as a glide; diphthongs beginning with u follow a velar consonant

stress.rule: Roots are stressed on the last vowel with few exceptions; prefixes are unstressed, suffixes and enclitics are either stressed or unstressed, and the last stressed morpheme of the word carries the main stress; stress that is not final is written with an acute accent, and a stressed nasal vowel with a tilde.
stress.cues: intensity and higher pitch according to Estigarribia (2020), who hears stressed syllables as not necessarily longer and clipped at the end of an utterance; Clopper & Tonhauser (2013) measured longer stressed syllables and steeper pitch movement under focus

rhythm.notes: Estigarribia (2020) describes every syllable as taking about the same time, with full vowels throughout; the last vowel of a phrase inside a sentence is often lengthened together with a pitch rise. No rhythm metrics have been published to my knowledge.

intonation.declarative: final fall; in short sentences either a rising accent on the first stressed word and a falling accent on the last (hat pattern) or rising accents on both (two-peak pattern)
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the second-position clitics =pa or =piko; usually said to end in a fall like a statement, without good phonetic studies
intonation.wh_question: question word with =pa or =piko; final fall, as for yes-no questions
intonation.continuation: marked pitch rise at the end of a phrase inside a sentence, often with lengthening of the last vowel
intonation.accent_shape: rising (L*+H) or falling (H+L*) movement on the stressed syllable; rising accents are preferred on a focused verb
intonation.notes: After Clopper & Tonhauser (2013) and the impressionistic sketch in Estigarribia (2020).

phonation: nasal voice over whole words or stretches of words (nasal harmony)

problems: no nasal harmony: only the vowels written with a tilde are nasal, and nothing spreads to neighbouring vowels or voiced consonants (porã comes out with an oral o and r)
the vowel /ɨ/ (y) uses the front rounded vowel of German ü (vowel file yy_4, IPA output y); its nasal partner ỹ uses a different, central and oral vowel file, so the pair neither matches nor is nasal
the puso is rendered as a short silence (phoneme _!) and not as a glottal stop
the modifier apostrophe U+02BC, which is often used for the puso, is not recognised and the word is spelled out letter by letter; only the ASCII apostrophe, U+2019 and U+02BB work
g̃ written with a combining tilde is read as plain g; the precomposed substitute ĝ is mapped to a retroflex nasal instead of the velar nasal or nasalised approximant
nd and nt are pronounced with a velar nasal ([ŋd], [ŋt]) instead of a dental one
v is pronounced as Spanish b ([b] or [β]) instead of the labiodental approximant [ʋ]
rr is a trill, not the retroflex sibilant of Paraguayan speech
good: stress on the last syllable by default, moved by the acute accent
nasal vowel phonemes for ã ẽ ĩ õ ũ
ch as [ʃ], j as a palatal fricative, r as a tap, g as an approximant or weak fricative between vowels
mb and ng as nasal plus stop

notes: Walker (1999) reports voice onset times for p, t, k in oral and nasal words; I could not check the figures and give no voice onset time block. Some speakers do not apply nasal harmony consistently to suffixes and enclitics (Estigarribia 2020).
